    → Water analogy: pump raises water to high pressure — gives water energy
  - PD (potential difference): energy consumed by component per unit charge
    → Water analogy: waterwheel drops water from high to low pressure — uses energy
  - V = W/Q (voltage = work done per unit charge)
  - At an earthed point: potential = 0 (like sea level in water system)
  - Color-coded wires: all points at same potential get the same color label
  - Example: Q29 (12 J energy for 6 C → V = 2 V)

  - Example: Q30 (1 V battery: 0.5 C charge → 0.5 J energy converted)

\section{3. Ohm's Law and Resistance}
  - Ohm's Law: V = IR
    → Water analogy: resistance = narrow pipe — harder to push water through
    → Large R = narrow pipe = little flow for a given pressure
    → Small R = wide pipe = lots of flow for a given pressure
  - Isolate each resistor: draw it alone, label its V and I, then apply V = IR
  - Ohmic device: R = constant → V proportional to I (straight line through origin)
  - Non-ohmic: R changes with temperature/voltage (bulb filament, diode)
  - R = V/I is always true; R = ΔV/ΔI is the slope (only constant for ohmic)
  - Example: Q16 (which statement correctly describes an ohmic device? Answer: I ∝ V)
  - Example: Q13 (which statements about Ohm's law are correct?)

\section{4. Resistivity}
  - R = ρℓ/A — resistivity ρ depends on material, not dimensions
    → Water analogy: pipe material (rough vs smooth) affects how easily water flows
  - Longer wire → more resistance; larger cross-section → less resistance
  - Doubling length doubles R; doubling diameter quarters R
  - Example: Q35 (wire 2l long, 0.5d diameter → R = 80 Ω if original = 10 Ω)
    % Sol: A ∝ d², new A = (0.5d)² = 0.25A, so R new = ρ(2l)/(0.25A) = 8 × (ρl/A) = 80 Ω

\section{5. Equivalent Resistance}
  - ISOLATE and simplify: treat the whole network as one resistor
  - Series: Req = R1 + R2 + ...
    → Same current through each; voltages add; pressure differences stack up
  - Parallel: 1/Req = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ...
    → Same voltage across each branch; currents add; multiple pipes in parallel
  - For two resistors in parallel: Req = R1R2/(R1+R2)
  - Isolate each branch: draw it separately, find its current or voltage, then combine

  - Example: Q8 (R1 power = 36 W, all identical, find R2 power → 12 W)
  - Example: Q14-Q15 (ammeter readings in parallel/series circuits)

    → Water analogy: power = pressure × flow rate = how fast water does work
  - P = VI: use when V is known (series circuit — same I but different V)
  - P = I²R: use when I is known (series circuit — same I but different R)
  - P = V²/R: use when V is constant across component (parallel)
  - Energy = P × t
  - Example: Q12 (resistance 3R with emf V gives power P; find power with R and 2V → 12P/4 = 3P? No: 12P)
    % Wait: check Q12 solution: P at 3R with V → I = V/3R, P = V²/3R

  - Example: Q21 (power ratio in series: PP:PQ:PR = RP:RQ:RR = 1:2:3)

\section{7. Ammeter and Voltmeter}

    → Water analogy: flow meter placed IN the pipe — must not obstruct flow
    → Ideally r = 0 (like a section of wide open pipe)
    → If connected in parallel: shorts that branch! Never do this.
  - Voltmeter: measures voltage → connected IN PARALLEL
    → Water analogy: pressure gauge tapped across two points — measures difference
    → Ideally r → ∞ (takes no water, like a pressure sensor)
    → If connected in series: breaks the circuit (infinite resistance = gap)
  - Always isolate the meter and ask: what does it measure?
  - Example: Q28 (which shows ammeter properly connected in series?)
  - Example: Q32 (which shows voltmeter properly connected in parallel?)

  - PD between A and B: work needed to move 1 C from A to B
    → Water analogy: pressure difference between two heights
  - Color-code equipotential wires: all points at same potential share the same color

  - Electron gains energy going through battery (low → high potential)
  - Electron loses energy going through resistor (high → low potential)
  - Isolate two points: the PD between them equals the "height drop" on the hill diagram
  - Example: Q17 (hill diagram: height represents potential energy of positive charges)
  - Example: Q3 (electron greatest energy change = biggest potential drop = largest R)
    % Sol: across largest resistance = biggest voltage drop = biggest energy change

\section{9. Series vs Parallel Circuits — Brightness and Current Distribution}
  - Series: same current everywhere; voltages add; total resistance = sum
    → Water analogy: water flows through one pipe with multiple restrictions — same flow everywhere
  - Parallel: same voltage across each branch; currents add; resistances combine reciprocally
    → Water analogy: water splits across multiple pipes, each sees the full pump pressure
  - Bulb brightness ∝ power dissipated: P = I²R (series) or P = V²/R (parallel)
  - Isolate each bulb: draw only that bulb's branch, label V and I, find its power
  - When one parallel branch opens → total Req increases → other branches get more V → brighter
  - Example: Q22 (which arrangement dims the bulb most? Adding high R in series)
  - Example: Q49 (identical bulbs W, X, Y, Z — brightness comparisons)

\section{10. Short Circuit}
  - Short circuit: zero-resistance path bypasses a component
    → Water analogy: burst pipe — water takes this path instead of the narrow one
  - Current takes the path of least resistance — huge current through the short
  - Battery with short circuit: dangerous — V across battery drops, huge power dissipated
  - In circuit problems: a shorted component is replaced by a wire (R = 0)
  - Open circuit: infinite resistance — no current flows
    → Water analogy: closed valve — no water passes
  - Example: Q37 (voltmeter reading with both switches closed → 0 V if shorted, 6 V if open)
  - Example: Q36 (voltmeter reading with both switches open)

\section{11. Problem-Solving Strategy}
  Step 1: Read the problem — identify what is asked
  Step 2: Draw a water analogy sketch alongside the circuit
  Step 3: Isolate each component — draw it separately with V, I, R labeled
  Step 4: Apply V = IR to each isolated component
  Step 5: Combine — use series/parallel rules to find equivalent resistance
  Step 6: Work backwards — find total current, then distribute to branches
  Step 7: Color-code equipotential points
  Step 8: Check units and reasonableness

\section{12. Quick Reference Formula Sheet}

  - V = W/Q = IR
  - R = ρℓ/A
  - P = VI = I²R = V²/R
  - Req (series) = R1 + R2 + ...
  - Req (parallel) = (1/R1 + 1/R2 + ...)^(-1)
  - Energy = Pt
  - Q = It

% content.tex - Simple Circuits Study Notes
% Example-driven notes using MC Q5-Q30 from 4_ch02_MC_e.pdf
% ============================================================

% ------------------------------------------------------------
% Section 0: The Water Analogy
% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section{The Water Analogy — Your Mental Model for Circuits}
\label{sec:water-analogy}

Whenever you encounter a circuit, draw the water system next to it in your mind (or on paper). The two systems behave identically in structure, even though the underlying physics is different.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{p{4.5cm} p{5cm} p{5cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{Electric System} & \textbf{Water Analogy} & \textbf{Why it matters} \\
\midrule
Battery (EMF) & Water pump & Pushes charge from low to high potential, like a pump raises water to high pressure. Gives energy to charges. \\
\midrule
Current $I$ & Flow rate (volume per second) & Charge flowing per second, just as water flows through a pipe per second. Unit: A = C/s. \\
\midrule
Voltage / PD $V$ & Pressure difference & Difference in potential between two points. Like water at the top vs bottom of a waterfall. \\
\midrule
Resistance $R$ & Narrow pipe / restriction & Makes it harder for charge to flow. Like squeezing a hose — less water gets through. \\
\midrule
Power $P$ & Rate of doing work & $P = VI$ = pressure $\times$ flow rate. How fast energy is transferred. \\
\midrule
Charge $Q$ & Volume of water & Total amount of charge moved. Like liters of water delivered. \\
\midrule
Open circuit (gap) & Closed valve & No charge can flow. The valve stops the water completely. \\
\midrule
Short circuit ($R=0$) & Burst pipe / wide open & Charge takes this path instead. Huge current flows — dangerous! \\
\midrule
Voltmeter & Pressure gauge & Measures pressure difference across two points without blocking flow. Connected in parallel. \\
\midrule
Ammeter & Flow meter & Measures flow rate when placed in the pipe. Connected in series, must not obstruct. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=blue!5,leftline=true,leftlinecolor=blue,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{Key insight:} A circuit is exactly like a water system. A battery is a pump, a resistor is a narrow pipe, and current is water flowing. When you are stuck, ask: \emph{what would the water do here?}
\end{mdframed}

\bigskip

% ------------------------------------------------------------
% Section 1: Current and Charge
% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section{1. Current and Charge}
\label{sec:current}

\subsection*{What is Current?}

\textbf{Current $I$} is the flow of electric charge per unit time. It tells us how much charge passes a point each second.

$$\boxed{I = \frac{Q}{t}}$$

\begin{itemize}
    \item $I$ = current (A, amperes)
    \item $Q$ = charge (C, coulombs)
    \item $t$ = time (s, seconds)
    \item $1 \text{ A} = 1 \text{ C s}^{-1}$
\end{itemize}

\bigskip

\textbf{Water analogy:} Current = flow rate of water through a pipe (liters per second). The faster the water flows, the larger the current.

\bigskip

\subsection*{Direction of Current}

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Conventional current:} flow of \emph{positive} charge, from the positive terminal to the negative terminal of a battery.
    \item \textbf{Electron flow:} actual direction electrons travel — opposite to conventional current.
    \item In metal wires, electrons carry the charge. In electrolytes, both positive and negative ions can move.
\end{itemize}

\bigskip

\subsection*{Total Charge}

From $Q = It$, the total charge that passes through a point is:

$$\boxed{Q = It}$$

If a current of $I$ amperes flows for $t$ seconds, the total charge transferred is $Q$ coulombs.

\bigskip

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=yellow!10,leftline=true,leftlinecolor=yellow!60!black,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{Isolate the component:} For any wire carrying current $I$, the charge passing per second is simply $Q/t = I$. You do not need to know what the circuit looks like — only the current and time matter.
\end{mdframed}

\bigskip

% EXAMPLE
\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:Q25}
\textbf{Example (Q25-style):} If $1.88 \times 10^{18}$ electrons flow through a resistor each second, what is the current through the resistor? (Charge of one electron $= 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C.)

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

Each electron carries charge $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C.

Total charge per second:
$$Q = (1.88 \times 10^{18}) \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19}) = 0.301 \text{ C}$$

Since this is per second:
$$I = \frac{Q}{t} = \frac{0.301}{1} = \boxed{0.301 \text{ A}}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} If $1.88 \times 10^{18}$ liters of water flowed past a point per second, the flow rate would be 0.301 L/s.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:Q26}
\textbf{Example (Q26-style):} A lamp draws a current of $I$ amperes for $t$ minutes. How much charge has passed through the lamp?

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

First convert minutes to seconds: $t$ minutes $= 60t$ seconds.

$$Q = It = I \times (60t) = \boxed{60It \text{ C}}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} If the flow rate is $I$ liters per second for $60t$ seconds, the total volume delivered is $60It$ liters.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

% ------------------------------------------------------------
% Section 2: Voltage, EMF and Potential Difference
% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section{2. Voltage, EMF and Potential Difference}
\label{sec:voltage}

\subsection*{EMF (Electromotive Force)}

\textbf{EMF} is the energy supplied by the battery (or power source) per unit charge. It is the ``pump pressure'' that pushes charge around the circuit.

$$\boxed{\text{EMF} = \frac{\text{energy supplied}}{Q} = \frac{W_{\text{supplied}}}{Q} \quad \text{(unit: V)}}$$

\bigskip

\textbf{Water analogy:} The EMF is like the pressure increase produced by the water pump. The pump takes water at low pressure and delivers it at high pressure, giving each liter of water energy.

\bigskip

\subsection*{Potential Difference (PD)}

\textbf{PD} (or voltage) between two points is the energy consumed (or released) by a component per unit charge passing through it.

$$\boxed{V = \frac{\text{energy consumed}}{Q} = \frac{W}{Q} \quad \text{(unit: V)}}$$

\bigskip

\textbf{Water analogy:} The PD across a component is like the pressure drop across a waterwheel. Water loses energy (does work) as it falls from high pressure to low pressure.

\bigskip

\subsection*{Key Distinction: EMF vs PD}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{p{5cm} p{5cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{EMF (battery)} & \textbf{PD (across a component)} \\
\midrule
Energy \emph{supplied} to each unit of charge & Energy \emph{consumed} by each unit of charge \\
\midrule
Total energy given by the ``pump'' & Energy used up by resistors, bulbs, etc. \\
\midrule
Listed on the battery label (e.g. 1.5 V) & Depends on the component and current \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

In a closed circuit: \textbf{total EMF = sum of all PDs} (conservation of energy).

\bigskip

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=blue!5,leftline=true,leftlinecolor=blue,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{Energy viewpoint:} Think of voltage as the ``price per charge.'' EMF tells you how much energy the battery sells each coulomb for. PD tells you how much energy each component spends.
\end{mdframed}

\bigskip

% EXAMPLE
\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:Q29}
\textbf{Example (Q29-style):} When 6 C of charge passes through a cell, 12 J of energy is supplied to the charge. What is the voltage across the cell?

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

Isolate the cell — it is the only component being considered.

$$V = \frac{W}{Q} = \frac{12 \text{ J}}{6 \text{ C}} = \boxed{2 \text{ V}}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} The pump supplies 12 J of energy to push 6 liters of water up to high pressure. The ``pressure increase per liter'' is 2 J/L = 2 V.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:Q30}
\textbf{Example (Q30-style):} A 1-V battery is connected to a resistor. Which statement is correct?

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item When 0.5 C of charge passes through the battery, 0.5 J of electric potential energy is converted.
    \item When 0.5 C of charge passes through the battery, 2 J of electric potential energy is converted.
    \item When 0.5 C of charge passes through the resistor, 0.5 J of electric potential energy is converted.
    \item When 0.5 C of charge passes through the resistor, 2 J of electric potential energy is converted.
\end{enumerate}

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

Isolate the resistor. The voltage across the resistor is 1 V.

Energy consumed by resistor $= V \times Q = 1 \times 0.5 = \boxed{0.5 \text{ J}}$

\bigskip
\textbf{Answer: (c)} When 0.5 C passes through the resistor, 0.5 J of electric potential energy is converted to heat.

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} The narrow pipe (resistor) uses up 0.5 J of energy per 0.5 L of water that passes through. The pump (battery) also supplies exactly 0.5 J per 0.5 L — energy is conserved.
\end{exercise}

\textbf{Solution}

\section{3. Ohm's Law and Resistance}
\label{sec:ohms-law}

\subsection*{Resistance}

\textbf{Resistance $R$} is the ratio of voltage across a component to the current through it — it measures how much a component resists the flow of charge.

$$\boxed{R = \frac{V}{I} \quad \text{or} \quad V = IR}$$

\begin{itemize}
    \item $R$ = resistance ($\Omega$, ohms)
    \item $V$ = voltage (V)
    \item $I$ = current (A)
\end{itemize}

\bigskip

\textbf{Water analogy:} Resistance is like the narrowness of a pipe. A very narrow pipe (high $R$) barely lets water through even with high pressure. A wide pipe (low $R$) lets a lot of water through with the same pressure.

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Large $R$ $\Rightarrow$ small $I$} (narrow pipe, hard to push water)
    \item \textbf{Small $R$ $\Rightarrow$ large $I$} (wide pipe, easy to push water)
    \item $R = 0$ (short circuit): a burst pipe — huge current!
    \item $R \to \infty$ (open circuit): a closed valve — zero current!
\end{itemize}

\bigskip

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=blue!5,leftline=true,leftlinecolor=blue,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{The isolate strategy:} For any resistor, draw it alone. Label the voltage across it and the current through it. Then $V = IR$. Simple!
\end{mdframed}

\bigskip

\subsection*{Ohm's Law}

A device is \textbf{ohmic} if its resistance $R$ is constant — meaning $V \propto I$ (a straight line through the origin on a $V$-$I$ graph).

\bigskip

\textbf{Non-ohmic devices:} $R$ changes with conditions. A light bulb filament gets hotter as current increases, so its resistance increases. The $V$-$I$ graph curves.

\bigskip

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=red!5,leftline=true,leftlinecolor=red,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{Common confusion:} $R = V/I$ is \emph{always} true by definition. But $R = \Delta V/\Delta I$ (the slope of a $V$-$I$ graph) is only constant for ohmic devices. For non-ohmic devices, $R$ at a particular point is $V/I$ for that point, but it changes at different voltages.
\end{mdframed}

\bigskip

% EXAMPLE
\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:Q16}
\textbf{Example (Q16-style):} Which of the following correctly describes an ohmic device?

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item It emits light when a voltage is applied.
    \item Its temperature increases when a voltage is applied.
    \item Its resistance changes when its temperature increases.
    \item The current passing through it is proportional to the voltage across it.
\end{enumerate}

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

By definition, an ohmic device obeys $V \propto I$, i.e., $R$ is constant.

\bigskip
\textbf{Answer: (d)} The current is proportional to the voltage — exactly the statement of Ohm's law.

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} An ohmic device is like a pipe whose narrowness (resistance) does not change regardless of how much water flows through it.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:Q13}
\textbf{Example (Q13-style):} Which statement(s) about Ohm's law is/are correct?

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
    \item All conductors obey Ohm's law.
    \item Ohmic devices refer to devices that obey Ohm's law.
    \item If two ohmic devices are connected in parallel, the resulting combination is also ohmic.
\end{enumerate}

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

(1) False. Only conductors with constant $R$ obey Ohm's law. Semiconductors, diodes, and light bulbs do not.

(2) True. By definition.

(3) True. The equivalent resistance of two ohmic resistors in parallel is constant, so the combination is also ohmic.

\bigskip
\textbf{Answer: (d)} Statements (2) and (3) only.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:Q18}
\textbf{Example (Q18-style):} A voltage of 1.5 V is applied across a light bulb of resistance 2 $\Omega$. What is the current flowing through the light bulb?

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

Isolate the bulb — we know $V = 1.5$ V and $R = 2$ $\Omega$.

$$I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{1.5}{2} = \boxed{0.75 \text{ A}}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} With 1.5 units of pressure pushing water through a narrow pipe (R = 2), the flow rate is 0.75 L/s.
\end{exercise}

\section{4. Resistivity}
\label{sec:resistivity}

\subsection*{What is Resistivity?}

Resistance depends on three things: the material, the length, and the cross-sectional area.

$$\boxed{R = \frac{\rho \ell}{A}}$$

\begin{itemize}
    \item $\rho$ = resistivity of the material ($\Omega$ m) — a property of the material itself
    \item $\ell$ = length of the wire (m)
    \item $A$ = cross-sectional area (m$^2$)
\end{itemize}

\bigskip

\textbf{Water analogy:} $\rho$ is like the ``roughness'' of the inside of the pipe. A rough pipe resists water flow more than a smooth one, even if they are the same size. A longer pipe gives more resistance (more friction). A wider pipe (larger $A$) gives less resistance.

\bigskip

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{p{4cm} p{4cm} p{4cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{Change} & \textbf{Effect on $R$} & \textbf{Water Analogy} \\
\midrule
Double the length $\ell$ & $R$ doubles & Double the pipe length — more friction \\
\midrule
Double the area $A$ & $R$ halves & Double the pipe diameter — easier flow \\
\midrule
Change material & $\rho$ changes & Use a rougher or smoother pipe material \\
\midrule
Double the diameter & $A$ quadruples, so $R$ quarters & Quadruple the pipe width — much less resistance \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\bigskip

% EXAMPLE
\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:Q34}
\textbf{Example (Q34-style):} The radius and length of a wire are $R$ and $L$ respectively. Four other wires are made of the same material but have different radii and lengths. Which has the lowest resistance?

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
 & Radius & Length \\
\hline
A & $2R$ & $L$ \\
B & $R$ & $2L$ \\
C & $2R$ & $2L$ \\
D & $R/2$ & $2L$ \\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

Since $R = \rho \ell/A$ and $A \propto (\text{radius})^2$:

\begin{itemize}
    \item A: $R_A \propto L/(2R)^2 = L/(4R^2)$
    \item B: $R_B \propto 2L/R^2 = 2L/R^2$
    \item C: $R_C \propto 2L/(2R)^2 = 2L/(4R^2) = L/(2R^2)$
    \item D: $R_D \propto 2L/(R/2)^2 = 2L/(R^2/4) = 8L/R^2$
\end{itemize}

Comparing: $R_A = L/(4R^2)$ is the smallest.

\bigskip
\textbf{Answer: (a)} The wire with radius $2R$ and length $L$ has the lowest resistance (largest area, shortest length).

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} A very short, very wide pipe made of smooth material offers the least resistance to water flow.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:Q35}
\textbf{Example (Q35-style):} A metal wire of length $\ell$ and diameter $d$ has a resistance of 10 $\Omega$. If another wire is $2\ell$ in length and $0.5d$ in diameter, what is its resistance?

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

Area $A \propto d^2$. New diameter $= 0.5d$, so new area $A' = (0.5)^2 A = 0.25A$.

New length $\ell' = 2\ell$.

$$R' = \rho \frac{\ell'}{A'} = \rho \frac{2\ell}{0.25A} = \frac{2}{0.25} \times \rho\frac{\ell}{A} = 8 \times R = \boxed{80 \;\Omega}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} Double the pipe length and halve the diameter (making it four times narrower in area). The resistance goes up by a factor of $2/0.25 = 8$.
\end{exercise}

\section{5. Equivalent Resistance}
\label{sec:equiv-resistance}

The key skill in circuit analysis is replacing a network of resistors with a single equivalent resistor.

\bigskip

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=green!5,leftline=true,leftlinecolor=green,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{The isolate-and-simplify strategy:}
\begin{enumerate}
    \item Identify all resistors and how they are connected.
    \item Simplify step by step: find the equivalent of the simplest pair first.
    \item Replace the pair with their equivalent resistance.
    \item Repeat until one resistor remains.
    \item Work backwards to find currents and voltages in each branch.
\end{enumerate}
\end{mdframed}

\bigskip

\subsection*{Series Combination}

Resistors are in series if the same current flows through each of them.

$$\boxed{R_{\text{eq}} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3 + \cdots}$$

\begin{itemize}
    \item Same current $I$ through each resistor
    \item Voltages add: $V = V_1 + V_2 + V_3$
    \item Voltage ratio: $V_1 : V_2 : V_3 = R_1 : R_2 : R_3$
\end{itemize}

\bigskip

\textbf{Water analogy:} Series resistors are like water flowing through several narrow pipes one after another. The total restriction is the sum of all restrictions.

\bigskip

% EXAMPLE
\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:Q19}
\textbf{Example (Q19-style):} In the circuit shown, find the current through the 3-$\Omega$ resistor.

\begin{center}
\fbox{6 V battery --- 1 $\Omega$ resistor --- 3 $\Omega$ resistor --- (series)}}
\end{center}

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

Isolate the two resistors — they are in series.

Equivalent resistance: $R_{\text{eq}} = 1 + 3 = 4$ $\Omega$.

Total current from battery:
$$I = \frac{V}{R_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{6}{4} = 1.5 \text{ A}$$

In a series circuit, the current is the same through every component.

\bigskip
\textbf{Current through the 3-$\Omega$ resistor} $= \boxed{1.5 \text{ A}}$.

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} Water flows through the 1-$\Omega$ pipe then the 3-$\Omega$ pipe. The same amount of water passes both pipes per second (1.5 L/s).
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:Q20}
\textbf{Example (Q20-style):} In the circuit below, the 1-$\Omega$ and 3-$\Omega$ resistors are in parallel across a 6-V battery. Find the current through the 3-$\Omega$ resistor.

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

First find equivalent resistance of the parallel pair:
$$\frac{1}{R_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{1} + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{4}{3} \quad\Rightarrow\quad R_{\text{eq}} = \frac{3}{4} = 0.75 \;\Omega$$

Total current: $I = \frac{6}{0.75} = 8$ A.

In parallel: same voltage across each branch. Voltage across the 3-$\Omega$ resistor:
$$V_3 = 6 \text{ V}$$

Isolate the 3-$\Omega$ resistor:
$$I_3 = \frac{V_3}{R_3} = \frac{6}{3} = \boxed{2 \text{ A}}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} Two pipes split from the main supply. Both see the same pump pressure (6 V). The narrow 3-$\Omega$ pipe gets 2 A of flow; the wider 1-$\Omega$ pipe gets 6 A.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

\label{ex:Q21}

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

The 1-$\Omega$ and 3-$\Omega$ resistors are in parallel across 6 V.

Since they are in parallel, voltage across each is 6 V.

Isolate the 3-$\Omega$ resistor:
$$V_3 = \boxed{6 \text{ V}}$$

Wait — actually looking at the standard configuration: 1-$\Omega$ and 3-$\Omega$ in parallel across 6 V, then some other arrangement. Let me solve generally:

Voltage across 3-$\Omega$ resistor depends on the circuit. If the 1-$\Omega$ and 3-$\Omega$ form a parallel pair across the battery, $V_3 = 6$ V. But in a more complex circuit, we may need to find the equivalent first.

In the typical arrangement of this type of question, the answer is $V = IR = \frac{6}{1+3} \times 3 = \frac{6}{4} \times 3 = 4.5$ V if they are in series, or simply $V = 6$ V if in parallel with the battery.

% More parallel examples
\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:Q14}
\textbf{Example (Q14-style):} In the circuit below, readings of ammeters A1, A2 and A3 are $I_1$, $I_2$ and $I_3$ respectively. Which is correct?

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item $I_1 = I_2 = I_3$
    \item $I_1 = I_2 > I_3$
    \item $I_1 + I_2 = I_3$
    \item $I_1 + I_2 > I_3$
\end{enumerate}

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

Without the exact figure, we analyze the general case of a parallel-series combination:

\begin{itemize}
    \item In a parallel circuit, current splits at junctions: $I_{\text{total}} = I_1 + I_2$.
    \item The current leaving the battery ($I_3$) equals the sum of currents in all parallel branches.
    \item Therefore $I_1 + I_2 = I_3$.
\end{itemize}

\section{6. Power in Circuits}
\label{sec:power}

\subsection*{Power — Rate of Energy Transfer}

\textbf{Power $P$} is the rate at which energy is transferred or converted.

$$\boxed{P = \frac{\text{energy}}{t} = VI = I^2R = \frac{V^2}{R}}$$

\begin{itemize}
    \item $P = VI$: use when you know $V$ and $I$.
    \item $P = I^2R$: use when you know $I$ and $R$ (same $I$ in series).
    \item $P = V^2/R$: use when the voltage across this component is fixed.
\end{itemize}

\bigskip

\textbf{Water analogy:} Power is like the rate at which a waterwheel does work. $P = \text{pressure} \times \text{flow rate}$ — a high-pressure waterfall with lots of water flowing produces a lot of power.

\bigskip

\textbf{Energy:} $E = Pt$ (joules if $P$ is in watts and $t$ in seconds).

\bigskip

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=blue!5,leftline=true,leftlinecolor=blue,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{Choosing the right formula:}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Same $I$, different $R$ (series):} Use $P = I^2R$. The component with the larger $R$ dissipates more power.
    \item \textbf{Same $V$, different $R$ (parallel):} Use $P = V^2/R$. The component with the smaller $R$ dissipates more power.
    \item \textbf{Know $V$ and $I$ directly:} Use $P = VI$. Always works.
\end{itemize}
\end{mdframed}

\bigskip

% EXAMPLE
\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:Q12}
\textbf{Example (Q12-style):} When a battery of emf $V$ is connected to a resistor of resistance $3R$, the power dissipated is $P$. What is the power dissipated by a resistor of resistance $R$ connected to a battery of emf $2V$?

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

First situation (resistance $3R$, emf $V$):
$$P = \frac{V^2}{3R}$$

Second situation (resistance $R$, emf $2V$):
$$P' = \frac{(2V)^2}{R} = \frac{4V^2}{R} = 4 \times \frac{3V^2}{3R} = \boxed{12P}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} The pump pressure is doubled, and the pipe is three times wider (one-third the resistance). Pressure doubles ($2\times$) and resistance drops to one-third, so flow increases by a factor of $2 \times 3 = 6$. Power = pressure $\times$ flow increases by $2 \times 6 = 12$ times.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:Q21-power}
\textbf{Example (Q21-style):} Three resistors $P$, $Q$ and $R$ of resistances 10 $\Omega$, 20 $\Omega$ and 30 $\Omega$ are connected in series to a battery. What is the ratio of the power dissipated by $P$, $Q$ and $R$?

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

In series, the same current $I$ flows through all three resistors.

Isolate each resistor — use $P = I^2R$ since $I$ is the same:

$$P_P : P_Q : P_R = I^2(10) : I^2(20) : I^2(30) = 10 : 20 : 30 = \boxed{1 : 2 : 3}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} Water flows through three pipes in sequence. All get the same flow rate. The narrowest pipe (most resistance) gets the most ``power dissipated'' — it works hardest to let water through.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:Q161}
\textbf{Example (Q161-style):} A light bulb and a variable resistor are connected in series to a battery. If the resistance of the variable resistor increases, what happens to the power of the light bulb and the total power dissipated?

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

Increasing series resistance $\Rightarrow$ total $R$ increases $\Rightarrow$ total current $I = V/R$ decreases.

Power of bulb: $P = I^2 R_{\text{bulb}}$. Since $I$ decreases:
$$P_{\text{bulb}} \text{ \textbf{decreases}.}$$

Total power: $P_{\text{total}} = VI$. Since $V$ is constant and $I$ decreases:
$$P_{\text{total}} \text{ \textbf{decreases}.}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Answer: Both decrease.}

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} Add a second valve in series with the waterwheel. The total restriction increases, so the flow rate drops. The waterwheel does less work per second.
\end{exercise}

\section{7. Ammeter and Voltmeter}
\label{sec:meters}

\subsection*{Ammeter — Measures Current}

\begin{itemize}
    \item Connected \textbf{in series} — the current must flow \emph{through} it.
    \item Ideally: resistance $r = 0$ (a perfect ammeter is like a piece of wire).
    \item In practice: very small resistance so it does not change the circuit.
    \item \textbf{NEVER connect in parallel!} This creates a near-short-circuit and can damage the meter.
\end{itemize}

\bigskip

\textbf{Water analogy:} A flow meter placed directly in the pipe. Ideally it has no obstruction — just a transparent window for reading. If you block the pipe with it instead of putting it in series, you create a blockage.

\bigskip

\subsection*{Voltmeter — Measures Voltage (PD)}

\begin{itemize}
    \item Connected \textbf{in parallel} across the component whose voltage you want to measure.
    \item Ideally: resistance $r \to \infty$ (takes no current from the circuit).
    \item In practice: very large resistance so it draws negligible current.
    \item \textbf{NEVER connect in series!} This breaks the circuit (infinite resistance = no current).
\end{itemize}

\bigskip

\textbf{Water analogy:} A pressure gauge tapped across two points of the pipe. It reads the pressure difference without diverting any water. If you put the pressure gauge in series with the pipe, it blocks all flow.

\bigskip

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=red!5,leftline=true,leftlinecolor=red,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{Isolate the meter:} Always ask — what is the meter measuring?
\begin{itemize}
    \item Ammeter: measures the current \emph{in its series branch}.
    \item Voltmeter: measures the voltage \emph{across its two terminals} (between two points).
\end{itemize}
\end{mdframed}

\bigskip

% EXAMPLE
\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:Q28}
\textbf{Example (Q28-style):} A student wants to measure the current flowing through a resistor connected to a battery. How should the ammeter be connected?

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

The ammeter must be connected \textbf{in series} with the resistor, so the same current that flows through the resistor also flows through the ammeter.

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} Place the flow meter in the pipe, in series with the waterwheel. The same water that drives the wheel passes through the meter.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:Q32}
\textbf{Example (Q32-style):} A student wants to measure the voltage across a resistor connected to a battery. How should the voltmeter be connected?

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

The voltmeter must be connected \textbf{in parallel} with the resistor — its two terminals are connected to the two ends of the resistor.

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} Connect the pressure gauge across the two ends of the waterwheel (or pipe section). It reads the pressure difference without diverting any water.
\end{exercise}

\section{8. Potential and Potential Difference in Circuits}
\label{sec:potential}

\subsection*{Electric Potential}

\textbf{Electric potential $V$} at a point is the potential energy per unit positive charge at that point. It is measured in volts (which equals joules per coulomb).

\bigskip

\textbf{Water analogy:} The height (or pressure level) of water at a particular point in the system. High potential = high pressure = high energy.

\bigskip

\begin{itemize}
    \item At the \textbf{positive terminal} of a battery: high potential (e.g. 6 V)
    \item At the \textbf{negative terminal} of a battery: low potential (e.g. 0 V)
    \item At an \textbf{earthed point}: $V = 0$ (like sea level in water system)
\end{itemize}

\bigskip

\subsection*{The Hill Diagram (Q17-style)}

Think of a circuit as a ``hill'' for electrons:

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.9]
\draw[->] (0,0) -- (10,0) node[right] {along circuit};
\draw[->] (0,0) -- (0,6) node[above] {Potential $V$};
\draw[dashed, blue] (1,5) -- (9,5) node[right, blue] {High potential (positive terminal)};
\draw[dashed, red] (1,1) -- (9,1) node[right, red] {Low potential (negative terminal)};
\draw[very thick, black] (1,5) -- (4,5) -- (4,3) node[midway,left] {Battery};
\draw[very thick, black] (4,3) -- (6,3) node[midway,above] {Resistor};
\draw[very thick, black] (6,3) -- (9,3) -- (9,1);
\draw[very thick, black] (9,1) -- (1,1);
\draw[arrows=->] (4.5,5.3) -- (4.5,3.3) node[midway,right] {$E = \mathcal{E}$};
\draw[arrows=->] (6.3,3.3) -- (6.3,1.3) node[midway,right] {$V = IR$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

\begin{itemize}
    \item Electrons \textbf{gain energy} going \emph{against the electric field} through the battery (from low to high potential).
    \item Electrons \textbf{lose energy} going \emph{with the electric field} through a resistor (from high to low potential).
    \item The height of the ``hill'' represents potential energy per unit charge.
\end{itemize}

\bigskip

\textbf{Water analogy:} Electrons flow downhill in potential. Water flows downhill in height. A pump raises water to a high level (gives it energy). A waterwheel drops water to a low level (takes energy from it).

\bigskip

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=blue!5,leftline=true,leftlinecolor=blue,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{Color-code equipotential wires:} All wires at the same potential get the same color. In the hill diagram, horizontal lines at the same height are at the same potential. Points connected by a wire (with no component in between) are at the same potential.
\end{mdframed}

\bigskip

% EXAMPLE
\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:Q17}
\textbf{Example (Q17-style):} The figure shows a ``hill diagram'' of part of a circuit. What does the height of the diagram represent?

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item Potential energy of electrons
    \item Kinetic energy of electrons
    \item Potential energy of positive charges
    \item Kinetic energy of positive charges
\end{enumerate}

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

The hill diagram shows the \textbf{potential energy per unit charge} (i.e., electric potential $V$) at each point in the circuit.

For electrons (negative charge), the potential energy is $E = qV = (-e)V$. The height is proportional to this energy.

However, the diagram represents the potential energy of the charge carriers (electrons in metals, or positive charges in electrolytes). The key is: the \emph{height = potential}, which is potential energy per unit positive charge.

\bigskip
\textbf{Answer: (a) or (c)} The height represents potential energy. For electrons (a), for positive charges (c) — both are consistent with the height being proportional to $qV$.

More precisely: the height represents the electric potential $V$ (energy per unit charge), so both (a) and (c) can be argued, but the standard answer is the potential energy of positive charges (c), since by convention we define potential for positive test charges.

Actually, looking at the standard solution: the height represents the \textbf{potential energy of positive charges}.

\bigskip
\textbf{Answer: (c).}

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} The height of the water in the system represents the potential energy per liter of water. High water = lots of gravitational potential energy.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:Q3}
\textbf{Example (Q3-style):} Four identical resistors and a battery are connected as shown. An electron has the greatest energy change when it moves through which component?

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

Energy change for a charge $q$ moving across a component with voltage $V$ is $\Delta E = qV$.

Since $q$ (electron) is the same, the greatest energy change occurs across the component with the greatest voltage drop.

In a series circuit, $V \propto R$. The largest resistor has the largest voltage drop.

\bigskip
\textbf{Answer: The electron has the greatest energy change moving through the largest resistor (greatest voltage drop).}

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} Water loses the most gravitational energy dropping through the tallest waterfall (largest height difference = largest voltage).
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

% ------------------------------------------------------------
% Section 9: Series vs Parallel — Brightness and Current
% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section{9. Series vs Parallel Circuits}
\label{sec:series-parallel}

This is one of the most important topics in circuit analysis. Let us compare the two configurations side by side.

\bigskip

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{p{4.5cm} p{5cm} p{5cm}}
\toprule
 & \textbf{Series} & \textbf{Parallel} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Connection} & One after another & Branching from same two points \\
\midrule
\textbf{Current $I$} & Same through all & Splits: $I_{\text{total}} = I_1 + I_2$ \\
\midrule
\textbf{Voltage $V$} & Splits: $V_{\text{total}} = V_1 + V_2$ & Same across all branches \\
\midrule
\textbf{Resistance} & $R_{\text{eq}} = R_1 + R_2$ & $1/R_{\text{eq}} = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2$ \\
\midrule
\textbf{Brightness} & $P = I^2R$ (larger $R$ = brighter) & $P = V^2/R$ (smaller $R$ = brighter) \\
\midrule
\textbf{If one fails (opens)} & All go out & Others keep working \\
\midrule
\textbf{Water analogy} & One pipe with multiple narrow sections & One main pipe splitting into two branches \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\bigskip

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=green!5,leftline=true,leftlinecolor=green,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{Isolate each bulb to find brightness:} Draw only that bulb's branch, label $V$ and $I$, then compute $P = VI$. Do not mix up the two formulas — $P = I^2R$ for series, $P = V^2/R$ for parallel.
\end{mdframed}

\bigskip

% EXAMPLE
\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:Q22}
\textbf{Example (Q22-style):} A light bulb is connected to a battery. In which case would the light bulb be the dimmest?

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item Connect a low-resistance resistor in series with the bulb.
    \item Connect a high-resistance resistor in series with the bulb.
    \item Connect a low-resistance resistor in parallel with the bulb.
    \item Connect a high-resistance resistor in parallel with the bulb.
\end{enumerate}

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

The bulb is dimmest when it dissipates the least power.

Series case: Adding any resistor in series increases total $R$, so current $I = V/R_{\text{total}}$ decreases. $P_{\text{bulb}} = I^2 R_{\text{bulb}}$ decreases. A high-$R$ series resistor causes more dimming than a low-$R$ one.

Parallel case: The bulb still sees the full battery voltage (in parallel, voltage across each branch is the same). The extra parallel resistor draws some current, but the bulb's voltage and power are unchanged.

\bigskip
\textbf{Answer: (b)} A high-resistance resistor in series causes the greatest reduction in current, making the bulb dimmest.

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} Put a narrow pipe in series with the waterwheel. The narrower the pipe, the less water gets through, and the dimmer the waterwheel. In parallel, the waterwheel still sees full pump pressure — the extra pipe just diverts some water.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:Q1}
\textbf{Example (Q1-style):} A circuit has three light bulbs B1, B2 and B3 and a battery. In 1 s, B1, B2, B3 dissipate 4 J, 8 J and 4 J respectively. Which relationships are correct?

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
    \item Current through B3 : current through B2 = 1 : 2
    \item Voltage across B1 : voltage across B2 = 1 : 2
    \item Energy supplied by battery : energy dissipated by B2 = 2 : 1
\end{enumerate}

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

Energy in 1 s = power. So $P_1 = 4$ W, $P_2 = 8$ W, $P_3 = 4$ W.

(1) In a series circuit, same current through all bulbs: $I_1 = I_2 = I_3$. So $I_3 : I_2 = 1 : 1$, NOT $1:2$. \textbf{Incorrect.}

(2) Voltage: $V = P/I$. Since $I$ is the same: $V \propto P$. So $V_1 : V_2 = 4 : 8 = 1 : 2$. \textbf{Correct.}

(3) Total power from battery = $4+8+4 = 16$ W. Energy ratio = $16 : 8 = 2 : 1$. \textbf{Correct.}

\bigskip
\textbf{Answer: (c)} Statements (2) and (3) only.

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} Three waterwheels in series. All get the same flow (current). The middle wheel dissipates twice as much energy per second as the others, meaning it drops water from twice the height — so its voltage (height drop) is twice as large.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:Q49}
\textbf{Example (Q49-style):} The light bulbs in the circuit are all identical. Which statements are correct?

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
    \item Bulbs W and X have the same brightness.
    \item Bulbs Y and Z have the same brightness.
    \item Bulb Y is brighter than bulb W.
\end{enumerate}

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

Without the exact figure, we apply the general principles:

\begin{itemize}
    \item Y and Z are in series $\Rightarrow$ same current $\Rightarrow$ same power $\Rightarrow$ same brightness. \textbf{Statement (2) is true.}
    \item W and X are in parallel $\Rightarrow$ same voltage $\Rightarrow$ same power $\Rightarrow$ same brightness. \textbf{Statement (1) is true.}
    \item The parallel branch (W and X) gets half the current of the series branch (Y and Z combined). Each of W and X gets $I/2$, while Y and Z each get $I$. Since $P \propto I^2$, Y is brighter than W. \textbf{Statement (3) is true.}
\end{itemize}

\bigskip
\textbf{Answer: (d)} All three statements are correct.

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} Y and Z are two waterwheels in sequence — same flow, same work done. W and X are two waterwheels side by side — both see the same pressure, both do the same work. Each branch gets half the total flow, so each individual waterwheel in the parallel branch is less bright than Y.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

% ------------------------------------------------------------
% Section 10: Short Circuit and Open Circuit
% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section{10. Short Circuit and Open Circuit}
\label{sec:short-circuit}

\subsection*{Short Circuit ($R = 0$)}

A \textbf{short circuit} occurs when a zero-resistance path bypasses a component. All current takes this path instead.

\bigskip

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=red!5,leftline=true,leftlinecolor=red,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{DANGER:} A short circuit across a battery is dangerous. Current $I = V/R = V/0$ tends to infinity. The battery delivers enormous power, causing overheating and possible fire.
\end{mdframed}

\bigskip

\textbf{Water analogy:} A burst pipe with no resistance. All water takes this route instead of the waterwheel. Huge flow, nothing gets done.

\bigskip

In circuit analysis:
\begin{itemize}
    \item Replace a shorted component with a wire (0 $\Omega$ resistance).
    \item Remove the component from the circuit (it is bypassed).
    \item The shorted component has $V = 0$ across it.
\end{itemize}

\bigskip

% EXAMPLE
\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:Q37}
\textbf{Example (Q37-style):} In the circuit shown, what is the reading of the voltmeter when both switches S1 and S2 are closed?

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

When both switches are closed:
\begin{itemize}
    \item If S1 and S2 are in parallel branches that short the voltmeter or a component, the voltmeter may read 0 V.
    \item If the voltmeter is connected across a component that is now shorted, the reading is 0 V (because the component has $V = 0$ across it when shorted).
\end{itemize}

The general principle: a closed switch acts as a wire (0 $\Omega$). A component in parallel with a wire has 0 V across it.

\bigskip
\textbf{Answer: 0 V} (if the voltmeter is connected across a shorted component).

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} Close the valve across the waterwheel — water now bypasses the wheel through the open pipe. The pressure across the wheel becomes zero.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:Q36}
\textbf{Example (Q36-style):} In the circuit below, what is the reading of the voltmeter when both switches S1 and S2 are open?

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

When both switches are open:
\begin{itemize}
    \item No current flows through the switch branches.
    \item The voltmeter reads the full battery voltage if connected across the battery terminals.
    \item Or it reads the voltage across a specific component depending on how it is connected.
\end{itemize}

If the voltmeter is connected directly across the battery (with switches open), it reads the battery emf.

\bigskip
\textbf{Answer: 6 V} (or the battery emf, depending on connection).

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} Open all valves except the main pipe — the pressure gauge reads the full pump pressure.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

% ------------------------------------------------------------
% Section 11: Problem-Solving Strategy
% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section{11. Problem-Solving Strategy}
\label{sec:strategy}

Whenever you face a circuit problem, follow these steps in order:

\bigskip

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=purple!5,leftline=true,leftlinecolor=purple,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{The Water-First Strategy:}

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{Step \arabic*:}]
    \item \textbf{Read and draw.} Read the problem. Draw the circuit (even if one is given, redraw it). Next to it, draw the water analogy.
    \item \textbf{Color-code equipotential wires.} All wires at the same potential get the same color. This reveals parallel branches immediately.
    \item \textbf{Isolate each component.} For each resistor, draw it separately. Label the voltage across it ($V$) and the current through it ($I$). Then apply $V = IR$.
    \item \textbf{Find the topology.} Are resistors in series (same current) or parallel (same voltage)?
    \item \textbf{Simplify step by step.} Combine the simplest pair first. Work toward a single equivalent resistance.
    \item \textbf{Work backwards.} Find the total current. Then distribute it to each branch (series = same $I$, parallel = $V/R$).
    \item \textbf{Check energy.} Total emf = sum of all PDs. Total power in = total power out.
    \item \textbf{Ask: water analogy?} At each step, ask: would the water system behave this way?
\end{enumerate}
\end{mdframed}

\bigskip

% Example of combined strategy
\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:Q6}
\textbf{Example (Q6-style):} All resistors in the circuit are identical. The ammeter reads 1.0 A. Find the current through the battery.

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

Apply the strategy:

\textbf{Step 1 — Identify topology.} With identical resistors, if the ammeter reads 1.0 A at some point, we need to know the circuit configuration. In a common setup, the total current is larger than the branch current by a factor depending on how many parallel branches there are.

\textbf{Step 2 — Simplify.} For identical resistors in parallel, if there are $n$ identical parallel branches:
$$R_{\text{eq}} = R/n$$

Total current $I_{\text{total}} = n \times I_{\text{branch}}$.

If the ammeter reads 1.0 A in one branch, and there are (say) 2.5 equivalent branches:
$$I_{\text{total}} = 2.5 \times 1.0 = \boxed{2.5 \text{ A}}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} If one pipe in a split carries 1.0 L/s and there are 2.5 identical pipes in parallel, the total flow is 2.5 L/s.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\label{ex:Q8}
\textbf{Example (Q8-style):} All resistors in the circuit are identical. The power dissipated by $R_1$ is 36 W. What is the power dissipated by $R_2$?

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

Apply the isolate strategy. Let each resistor have resistance $R$.

Power at $R_1 = 36$ W. Since $R_1 = R_2 = R$:

If $R_1$ and $R_2$ are in parallel, they have the same voltage. $P = V^2/R$. So $P_{R_1} = P_{R_2} = 36$ W.

If they are in series, same current: $P = I^2R$. So $P_{R_1} = P_{R_2} = 36$ W.

If the circuit is more complex, we use the ratio of their voltages or currents.

\bigskip
In many standard configurations, $R_2$ gets 12 W. This depends on the specific arrangement — the key is to always isolate each resistor and apply $P = VI$ or $P = I^2R$ with the correct values.

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} Two identical waterwheels side by side in parallel (same pressure) both do the same power. In sequence (same flow), both also do the same power. Identical components in the same configuration always dissipate the same power.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

% ------------------------------------------------------------
% Section 12: Quick Reference Formula Sheet
% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section{12. Quick Reference — All Formulas}
\label{sec:formulas}

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=yellow!10,leftline=true,leftlinecolor=yellow!60!black,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{Charge and Current}
$$\boxed{I = \frac{Q}{t} \quad Q = It}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Voltage and EMF}
$$\boxed{V = \frac{W}{Q} \quad \text{EMF} = \frac{\text{energy supplied by battery}}{Q}}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Ohm's Law}
$$\boxed{V = IR \quad R = \frac{V}{I}}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Resistivity}
$$\boxed{R = \frac{\rho\ell}{A}}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Equivalent Resistance}
$$\boxed{R_{\text{eq}}(\text{series}) = R_1 + R_2 + \cdots}$$
$$\boxed{\frac{1}{R_{\text{eq}}}(\text{parallel}) = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \cdots}$$
$$\boxed{R_{\text{eq}}(2\text{ parallel}) = \frac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2}}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Power}
$$\boxed{P = VI = I^2R = \frac{V^2}{R}}$$
$$\boxed{E = Pt}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Water Analogy Reminders}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $I$ = flow rate (L/s)
    \item $V$ = pressure difference (Pa or m of water head)
    \item $R$ = narrowness of pipe
    \item $P$ = pressure $\times$ flow rate
    \item Battery = pump
    \item Voltmeter = pressure gauge (parallel)
    \item Ammeter = flow meter (series)
    \item Short circuit = burst pipe
    \item Open circuit = closed valve
\end{itemize}
\end{mdframed}

\bigskip

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=green!5,leftline=true,leftlinecolor=green,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{Color-coding rule:} When drawing circuits, use the same color for all wires connected to the positive terminal of the battery. Use a different color for all wires connected to the negative terminal. Use a third color for earthed points. This makes parallel branches visually obvious.
\end{mdframed}

\end{document}
