% ------------------------------------------------------------
% Section 0: What do we need to measure in a circuit?
% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section*{The Starting Point — What Do We Measure in a Circuit?}

When we analyse a circuit, we always care about three quantities. Let's meet them through a real question.

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Q1 (HKDSE 2022 Ch2 MC):} The figure shows a circuit with three light bulbs B1, B2 and B3 and a battery. In 1 s, B1, B2 and B3 dissipate energy of 4 J, 8 J and 4 J respectively. Which relationships are correct?

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
    \item Current through B3 : current through B2 = 1 : 2
    \item Voltage across B1 : voltage across B2 = 1 : 2
    \item Energy supplied by the battery : energy dissipated by B2 = 2 : 1
\end{enumerate}

A. (1) and (2) only \quad B. (1) and (3) only \quad C. (2) and (3) only \quad D. (1), (2) and (3)

\bigskip
\textbf{Let's solve it — and in doing so, discover what current, voltage and energy are.}

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 1 — Energy per second = Power.}

Since all three bulbs dissipate energy in 1 s:
$$P_1 = 4\text{ W},\quad P_2 = 8\text{ W},\quad P_3 = 4\text{ W}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 2 — What does "series" tell us about current?}

If the three bulbs are in series, the same current flows through all of them. So:
$$I_3 : I_2 = 1 : 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \textbf{Statement (1) is FALSE.}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 3 — Voltage in a series circuit.}

In series, the same current $I$ flows through each. Since $P = VI$, we get $V = P/I$. Because $I$ is the same for all:
$$V_1 : V_2 = P_1 : P_2 = 4 : 8 = 1 : 2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \textbf{Statement (2) is TRUE.}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 4 — Total energy from the battery.}

Total power supplied = $4 + 8 + 4 = 16$ W, so in 1 s the battery supplies 16 J.

Energy ratio = $16 : 8 = 2 : 1$ \quad\Rightarrow\quad \textbf{Statement (3) is TRUE.}

\bigskip
\textbf{Answer: C — statements (2) and (3) only.}

\bigskip
\textbf{What did we just learn?} Three new words appeared: current ($I$), voltage ($V$) and power ($P$). We also learned the key fact that in a series circuit, current is the same everywhere. This gives us our first mental model.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

% WATER ANALOGY INTRODUCED HERE
\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=blue!5,leftline=true,linecolor=blue,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{The Water Analogy — your mental model for everything that follows.}

\bigskip
Before reading each section, draw the water system next to the circuit in your mind. They behave identically in structure.

\bigskip
\begin{tabular}{p{4cm} p{5.5cm} p{5.5cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{Electric} & \textbf{Water Analogy} & \textbf{What it means} \\
\midrule
Battery (pushes charge) & Water pump & Raises water to high pressure. Gives energy to each litre. \\
\midrule
Current $I$ (charge per second) & Flow rate (litres/second) & How much charge passes a point each second. Unit: A = C/s. \\
\midrule
Voltage $V$ (energy per charge) & Pressure difference & How much energy each litre of water carries between two points. \\
\midrule
Resistance $R$ (obstructs flow) & Narrow pipe & Makes it harder for water to get through. More resistance = less flow. \\
\midrule
Power $P$ (energy/second) & Pressure $\times$ flow rate & How fast energy is transferred. $P = VI$. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{mdframed}

\bigskip

% ------------------------------------------------------------
% Section 1: Current and Charge
% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section{1. Current — How Much Charge Flows Each Second}

Let's meet current through another real question.

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Q25 (HKDSE Ch2 MC):} If $1.88 \times 10^{18}$ electrons flow through a resistor each second, what is the current through the resistor? (Charge of one electron $= 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C.)

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 1 — How much charge flows per second?}

Each electron carries $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C of charge.

Total charge per second:
$$Q = (1.88 \times 10^{18}) \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19}) = 0.301 \text{ C}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 2 — Current is charge per second.}

By definition:
$$\boxed{I = \frac{Q}{t}}$$

Since this is the charge flowing in 1 second:
$$I = \frac{0.301}{1} = \boxed{0.301 \text{ A}}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} $1.88 \times 10^{18}$ electrons per second is like $1.88 \times 10^{18}$ litres of water per second flowing through a pipe. The flow rate is 0.301 L/s.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

This gives us the definition:

$$\boxed{I = \frac{Q}{t} \qquad Q = It}$$

where $I$ = current (A), $Q$ = charge (C), $t$ = time (s).

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Q26 (HKDSE Ch2 MC):} A lamp draws a current of $I$ amperes for $t$ minutes. How much charge has passed through the lamp?

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

Convert minutes to seconds: $t$ minutes $= 60t$ seconds.

$$Q = I \times (60t) = \boxed{60It \text{ C}}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Key trick:} Always convert units before plugging in. Minutes $\to$ seconds, milliamps $\to$ amps, etc.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=yellow!10,leftline=true,linecolor=yellow!60!black,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{Isolate the component:} For any wire carrying current $I$, the charge passing per second is $Q/t = I$. You only need the current and time — not the rest of the circuit.
\end{mdframed}

\bigskip

\textbf{Direction of current:} In metal wires, electrons (negative charge) flow. By convention, we label current as the flow of positive charge — from the positive to the negative terminal. This is called \textbf{conventional current} and is what we use in all circuit problems.

\bigskip

% ------------------------------------------------------------
% Section 2: Voltage, EMF and Potential Difference
% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section{2. Voltage — How Much Energy Each Charge Carries}

Voltage is the most important and most confusing concept in circuits. Let's understand it through a problem.

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Q30 (HKDSE Ch2 MC):} A 1-V battery is connected to a resistor. Which statement is correct?

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item When 0.5 C of charge passes through the battery, 0.5 J of electric potential energy is converted.
    \item When 0.5 C of charge passes through the battery, 2 J of electric potential energy is converted.
    \item When 0.5 C of charge passes through the resistor, 0.5 J of electric potential energy is converted.
    \item When 0.5 C of charge passes through the resistor, 2 J of electric potential energy is converted.
\end{enumerate}

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 1 — What does "1 V" mean?}

1 V means: each coulomb of charge gains or loses 1 joule of energy when it passes through this component.

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 2 — Energy gained/lost = $V \times Q$.}

The battery gives 1 J of energy to each coulomb that passes through it. For 0.5 C:
$$\text{Energy at battery} = 1 \times 0.5 = 0.5 \text{ J}$$

The resistor consumes 1 J of energy per coulomb that passes through it. For 0.5 C:
$$\text{Energy at resistor} = 1 \times 0.5 = 0.5 \text{ J}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Answer: (c)} When 0.5 C passes through the resistor, 0.5 J of energy is converted to heat.

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} The pump (battery) pushes 0.5 litres of water through, giving each litre 1 J of energy (1 V). The narrow pipe (resistor) uses up 1 J per litre — 0.5 J for 0.5 L. Energy is conserved: the pump gives exactly what the resistor uses.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

This gives us the definition of voltage (potential difference):

$$\boxed{V = \frac{W}{Q} \qquad \text{energy transferred} = V \times Q}$$

where $V$ = voltage (V = J/C), $W$ = energy (J), $Q$ = charge (C).

\bigskip

Now let's look at the battery side — EMF.

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Q29 (HKDSE Ch2 MC):} When 6 C of charge passes through a cell, 12 J of energy is supplied to the charge. What is the voltage across the cell?

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

Isolate the cell. It is the source of energy here.

$$V = \frac{W}{Q} = \frac{12 \text{ J}}{6 \text{ C}} = \boxed{2 \text{ V}}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} The pump supplies 12 J of energy to push 6 litres of water to high pressure. The ``pressure increase per litre'' is 12/6 = 2 J/L = 2 V.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Q31 (HKDSE Ch2 MC):} When $3 \times 10^{19}$ electrons pass through a battery, 18 J of energy is supplied to them. What is the voltage across the battery? (Charge of electron $= 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C.)

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

Step 1: Total charge: $Q = (3 \times 10^{19}) \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19}) = 4.8$ C.

Step 2: Isolate the battery — energy supplied is 18 J:
$$V = \frac{W}{Q} = \frac{18}{4.8} = \boxed{3.75 \text{ V}}$$
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=blue!5,leftline=true,linecolor=blue,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{EMF vs PD — what's the difference?}

Both are measured in volts. But:

\bigskip
\begin{tabular}{p{4cm} p{5.5cm} p{5.5cm}}
\toprule
 & \textbf{EMF (battery)} & \textbf{PD (across a component)} \\
\midrule
Energy & Energy \emph{supplied} to each coulomb & Energy \emph{consumed} by each coulomb \\
\midrule
Where & At the battery & At resistors, bulbs, etc. \\
\midrule
Formula & EMF = $W_{\text{supplied}}/Q$ & PD = $W_{\text{consumed}}/Q$ \\
\midrule
Total & Total EMF = sum of all PDs (energy conservation) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

\bigskip
\textbf{Key rule:} In a closed circuit: \textbf{total EMF = sum of all PDs.} This is non-negotiable — it comes from conservation of energy.
\end{mdframed}

\bigskip

% ------------------------------------------------------------
% Section 3: Ohm's Law and Resistance
% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section{3. Resistance — Why Do Some Components Obstruct Current?}

What does resistance actually do? Let's see.

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Q18 (HKDSE Ch2 MC):} A voltage of 1.5 V is applied across a light bulb of resistance 2 $\Omega$. What is the current flowing through the light bulb?

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

Isolate the bulb — we know $V = 1.5$ V and $R = 2$ $\Omega$.

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 1 — What is resistance?}

Resistance is the ratio of voltage to current. It tells us how much voltage is needed to push a given current through a component.

$$R = \frac{V}{I} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \boxed{V = IR}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 2 — Rearrange for current.}
$$I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{1.5}{2} = \boxed{0.75 \text{ A}}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} With 1.5 units of pressure (1.5 V) pushing water through a narrow pipe of resistance 2, the flow rate is 0.75 L/s.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

The three equivalent forms of Ohm's Law:
$$\boxed{V = IR \qquad I = \frac{V}{R} \qquad R = \frac{V}{I}}$$

\bigskip

What does resistance actually mean physically?

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Large $R$ $\Rightarrow$ small $I$}: narrow pipe, hard to push water through.
    \item \textbf{Small $R$ $\Rightarrow$ large $I$}: wide pipe, easy for water to flow.
    \item $R = 0$ (short circuit): burst pipe — enormous current!
    \item $R \to \infty$ (open circuit): closed valve — zero current.
\end{itemize}

\bigskip

Now — what does "ohmic" mean?

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Q16 (HKDSE Ch2 MC):} Which of the following correctly describes an ohmic device?

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item It emits light when a voltage is applied.
    \item Its temperature increases when a voltage is applied.
    \item Its resistance changes when its temperature increases.
    \item The current passing through it is proportional to the voltage across it.
\end{enumerate}

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

By definition, an \textbf{ohmic device} obeys $V \propto I$, i.e. $R$ is constant regardless of voltage or current.

\textbf{Answer: (d)} The current is proportional to the voltage — exactly $V = IR$ with constant $R$.

\bigskip
\textbf{Key distinction:} A light bulb filament is non-ohmic. As current increases, the filament gets hot and its resistance increases. The $V$-$I$ graph curves.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Q13 (HKDSE Ch2 MC):} Which statement(s) about Ohm's law is/are correct?

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
    \item All conductors obey Ohm's law.
    \item Ohmic devices refer to devices that obey Ohm's law.
    \item If two ohmic devices are connected in parallel, the resulting combination is also ohmic.
\end{enumerate}

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

(1) False. Only conductors with constant $R$ obey Ohm's law. Semiconductors, diodes, and light bulbs do not.

(2) True. By definition.

(3) True. The equivalent resistance of two constant-$R$ resistors in parallel is also constant, so the combination is ohmic.

\bigskip
\textbf{Answer: (d)} Statements (2) and (3) only.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=red!5,leftline=true,linecolor=red,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{Common mistake about $R = V/I$:} This ratio is \emph{always} true by definition. But when we look at a $V$-$I$ graph, the slope $\Delta V/\Delta I$ is only constant for ohmic devices. For non-ohmic devices, the resistance at a particular point is $V/I$ for that point — but it changes at different voltages.
\end{mdframed}

\bigskip

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=blue!5,leftline=true,linecolor=blue,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{The isolate strategy:} For any resistor, draw it alone. Label the voltage across it and the current through it. Then $V = IR$. Simple!
\end{mdframed}

\bigskip

% ------------------------------------------------------------
% Section 4: Resistivity
% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section{4. Resistivity — What Determines a Wire's Resistance?}

Why does resistance depend on the wire itself? Let's find out.

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Q34 (HKDSE Ch2 MC):} A wire has radius $R$ and length $L$. Four other wires are made of the same material but have different radii and lengths. Which has the lowest resistance?

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
 & Radius & Length \\
\hline
A & $2R$ & $L$ \\
B & $R$ & $2L$ \\
C & $2R$ & $2L$ \\
D & $R/2$ & $2L$ \\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

Resistance depends on three things: material (resistivity $\rho$), length $\ell$, and cross-sectional area $A$.

$$\boxed{R = \frac{\rho \ell}{A}}$$

Since all wires are the same material, $\rho$ is the same. We only compare $\ell$ and $A$.

Note: $A \propto (\text{radius})^2$.

\begin{itemize}
    \item A: $R_A \propto \dfrac{L}{(2R)^2} = \dfrac{L}{4R^2}$
    \item B: $R_B \propto \dfrac{2L}{R^2} = \dfrac{2L}{R^2}$
    \item C: $R_C \propto \dfrac{2L}{(2R)^2} = \dfrac{2L}{4R^2} = \dfrac{L}{2R^2}$
    \item D: $R_D \propto \dfrac{2L}{(R/2)^2} = \dfrac{2L}{R^2/4} = \dfrac{8L}{R^2}$
\end{itemize}

Comparing: $R_A = \dfrac{L}{4R^2}$ is the smallest.

\bigskip
\textbf{Answer: (a)} The wire with radius $2R$ (doubled radius = quadrupled area) and length $L$ (shortest) has the lowest resistance.

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} $\rho$ is the roughness of the pipe interior. A longer pipe has more friction. A wider pipe (larger $A$) has less friction per litre. Doubling the diameter quadruples the area and quarters the resistance.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

Practical consequences:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{p{4cm} p{4cm} p{5cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{Change} & \textbf{Effect on $R$} & \textbf{Water Analogy} \\
\midrule
Double length $\ell$ & $R$ doubles & Double pipe length — more friction \\
\midrule
Double area $A$ & $R$ halves & Double pipe diameter — easier flow \\
\midrule
Double diameter & $A$ quadruples, $R$ quarters & Four times wider — much less resistance \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Q35 (HKDSE Ch2 MC):} A wire of length $\ell$ and diameter $d$ has resistance 10 $\Omega$. If another wire is $2\ell$ in length and $0.5d$ in diameter, what is its resistance?

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

New diameter $= 0.5d$, so new area $A' = (0.5)^2 A = 0.25A$.

New length $\ell' = 2\ell$.

$$R' = \rho \frac{\ell'}{A'} = \rho \frac{2\ell}{0.25A} = \frac{2}{0.25} \times \rho\frac{\ell}{A} = 8 \times R = \boxed{80\;\Omega}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} Double the pipe length and halve its diameter (making it four times narrower in area). The resistance goes up by $2/0.25 = 8$ times.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

% ------------------------------------------------------------
% Section 5: Equivalent Resistance
% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section{5. Equivalent Resistance — Simplifying Circuits}

How do we reduce a complex circuit to one number? Let's find out.

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Q19 (HKDSE Ch2 MC):} A 6 V battery is connected in series with a 1-$\Omega$ resistor and a 3-$\Omega$ resistor. Find the current through the 3-$\Omega$ resistor.

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 1 — Are these in series?} Yes. The same current flows through both resistors.

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 2 — Series equivalent resistance.}
$$\boxed{R_{\text{eq}} = R_1 + R_2 + \cdots}$$

$$R_{\text{eq}} = 1 + 3 = 4\;\Omega$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 3 — Total current from the battery.}
$$I = \frac{V}{R_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{6}{4} = 1.5\text{ A}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 4 — In series, current is the same everywhere.}
$$\text{Current through the 3-$\Omega$ resistor} = \boxed{1.5\text{ A}}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} Two narrow pipes in sequence. Both carry the same flow (1.5 L/s). The total restriction is the sum: 1 + 3 = 4 units of resistance.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

What about parallel?

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Q20 (HKDSE Ch2 MC):} A 6 V battery is connected with a 1-$\Omega$ resistor and a 3-$\Omega$ resistor in parallel. Find the current through the 3-$\Omega$ resistor.

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 1 — Are these in parallel?} Yes. Both are connected directly across the battery — same voltage across each.

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 2 — Parallel equivalent resistance.}
$$\frac{1}{R_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} = \frac{1}{1} + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{4}{3}$$
$$R_{\text{eq}} = \frac{3}{4} = 0.75\;\Omega$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 3 — Total current from battery.}
$$I_{\text{total}} = \frac{V}{R_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{6}{0.75} = 8\text{ A}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 4 — Voltage across each parallel branch is the same (= battery voltage = 6 V).}

Isolate the 3-$\Omega$ resistor:
$$I_3 = \frac{V_3}{R_3} = \frac{6}{3} = \boxed{2\text{ A}}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} Two pipes split from the same pump. Both see the same pump pressure (6 V). The narrow 3-$\Omega$ pipe gets 2 A of flow; the wider 1-$\Omega$ pipe gets 6 A. Total flow = 2 + 6 = 8 A.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

The key parallel formula for two resistors:

$$\boxed{R_{\text{eq}}(2\text{ parallel}) = \frac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2}}$$

\bigskip

Key rules for series and parallel:

\bigskip
\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=green!5,leftline=true,linecolor=green,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{Series: same current through each.}

\bigskip
\begin{tabular}{p{3cm} p{6cm}}
\midrule
Current & $I_1 = I_2 = I$ (same) \\
\midrule
Voltage & $V = V_1 + V_2$ (adds up) \\
\midrule
Voltage ratio & $V_1 : V_2 = R_1 : R_2$ \\
\midrule
Resistance & $R_{\text{eq}} = R_1 + R_2$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

\bigskip
\textbf{Parallel: same voltage across each.}

\bigskip
\begin{tabular}{p{3cm} p{6cm}}
\midrule
Voltage & $V_1 = V_2 = V$ (same) \\
\midrule
Current & $I = I_1 + I_2$ (splits) \\
\midrule
Current ratio & $I_1 : I_2 = 1/R_1 : 1/R_2$ \\
\midrule
Resistance & $1/R_{\text{eq}} = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{mdframed}

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Q21 (HKDSE Ch2 MC):} Find the voltage across the 3-$\Omega$ resistor when it is in parallel with a 1-$\Omega$ resistor across a 6-V battery.

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

In parallel, the voltage across each branch is the same as the battery voltage:
$$V_3 = \boxed{6\text{ V}}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} Both pipes branch from the same pump. Both see the full pump pressure of 6 units.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

% ------------------------------------------------------------
% Section 6: Power in Circuits
% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section{6. Power — How Fast is Energy Being Transferred?}

Let's tackle power through a real question.

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Q12 (HKDSE Ch2 MC):} When a battery of emf $V$ is connected to a resistor of resistance $3R$, the power dissipated is $P$. What is the power dissipated by a resistor of resistance $R$ connected to a battery of emf $2V$?

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 1 — Power formula.}

$$P = VI = \frac{V^2}{R}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 2 — First situation: $R_1 = 3R$, $V_1 = V$.}
$$P = \frac{V^2}{3R}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 3 — Second situation: $R_2 = R$, $V_2 = 2V$.}
$$P' = \frac{(2V)^2}{R} = \frac{4V^2}{R} = 4 \times \frac{3V^2}{3R} = \boxed{12P}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} Double the pump pressure ($2\times$) and reduce the pipe resistance to one-third ($R \to R/3$, i.e. three times wider). Pressure doubles and resistance drops to a third, so flow increases by $2 \times 3 = 6$ times. Power = pressure $\times$ flow increases by $2 \times 6 = 12$ times.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

The three power formulas (all equivalent — use the one that fits your knowns):

$$\boxed{P = VI = I^2R = \frac{V^2}{R}}$$

Energy: $E = Pt$ (joules if $P$ is in watts and $t$ in seconds).

\bigskip

How to choose which formula to use:

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=blue!5,leftline=true,linecolor=blue,linewidth=2pt]
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Same $I$, different $R$ (series):} Use $P = I^2R$. The larger $R$ dissipates more power.
    \item \textbf{Same $V$, different $R$ (parallel):} Use $P = V^2/R$. The smaller $R$ dissipates more power.
    \item \textbf{Know $V$ and $I$ directly:} Use $P = VI$. Always works.
\end{itemize}
\end{mdframed}

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Q (HKDSE Ch2 MC):} Three resistors $P$, $Q$ and $R$ of resistances 10 $\Omega$, 20 $\Omega$ and 30 $\Omega$ are connected in series to a battery. What is the ratio of the power dissipated by $P$, $Q$ and $R$?

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

In series, the same current $I$ flows through all three resistors.

Use $P = I^2R$ since $I$ is the same for all:
$$P_P : P_Q : P_R = I^2(10) : I^2(20) : I^2(30) = 10 : 20 : 30 = \boxed{1 : 2 : 3}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} Water flows through three pipes in sequence. All get the same flow rate. The narrowest pipe (most resistance) dissipates the most power — it does the most ``work'' per second.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Q (HKDSE Ch2 MC):} A light bulb and a variable resistor are connected in series to a battery. If the resistance of the variable resistor increases, what happens to the power of the light bulb and the total power dissipated?

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

Increasing series resistance $\Rightarrow$ total $R$ increases $\Rightarrow$ total current $I = V/R$ decreases.

\bigskip
\textbf{Power of bulb:} $P_{\text{bulb}} = I^2 R_{\text{bulb}}$. Since $I$ decreases and $R_{\text{bulb}}$ is unchanged:
$$P_{\text{bulb}} \text{ \textbf{decreases}.}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Total power:} $P_{\text{total}} = VI$. Since $V$ is constant and $I$ decreases:
$$P_{\text{total}} \text{ \textbf{decreases}.}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Answer: Both decrease.}

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} Add a second valve in series with the waterwheel. The total restriction increases, so the flow rate drops. Both the waterwheel and the total system do less work per second.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

% ------------------------------------------------------------
% Section 7: Ammeter and Voltmeter
% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section{7. Ammeter and Voltmeter — How Do We Measure in a Circuit?}

How should meters be connected? Let's find out.

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Q28 (HKDSE Ch2 MC):} A student wants to measure the current flowing through a resistor connected to a battery. How should the ammeter be connected?

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

An ammeter measures \textbf{current} (charge per second). Current must flow \emph{through} it, so it goes in series with the resistor.

\bigskip
\textbf{Answer: Connect the ammeter in series with the resistor.}

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} A flow meter placed directly in the pipe, in series with the waterwheel. The same water that drives the wheel passes through the meter. If you put the flow meter across the pipe (parallel), you block the pipe.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Q32 (HKDSE Ch2 MC):} A student wants to measure the voltage across a resistor connected to a battery. How should the voltmeter be connected?

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

A voltmeter measures \textbf{voltage} (energy per charge). Voltage exists between two points, so the voltmeter connects its two terminals across those two points — that is, in parallel with the component.

\bigskip
\textbf{Answer: Connect the voltmeter in parallel with the resistor.}

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} A pressure gauge tapped across the two ends of the pipe. It reads the pressure difference without diverting any water. If you put the pressure gauge in series with the pipe, it blocks all flow (infinite resistance).
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

Key properties of each meter:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{p{3.5cm} p{4.5cm} p{4.5cm} p{3.5cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{Meter} & \textbf{Quantity} & \textbf{Connection} & \textbf{Ideal $R$} \\
\midrule
Ammeter & Current (A) & Series & $R = 0$ (like a wire) \\
\midrule
Voltmeter & Voltage (V) & Parallel & $R = \infty$ (no current taken) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\bigskip

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=red!5,leftline=true,linecolor=red,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{NEVER connect:}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Ammeter in parallel $\Rightarrow$ near-short-circuit, can damage the meter and circuit.
    \item Voltmeter in series $\Rightarrow$ breaks the circuit, reads the battery emf instead.
\end{itemize}
\end{mdframed}

\bigskip

% ------------------------------------------------------------
% Section 8: Potential and Potential Difference
% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section{8. Potential Difference in Circuits — Tracing the Energy Changes}

Let's use the potential concept to understand energy changes in a circuit.

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Q3 (HKDSE Ch2 MC):} Four identical resistors and a battery are connected as shown. An electron has the greatest energy change when it moves through which component?

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

Energy change for a charge $q$ moving across a component with voltage $V$ is:
$$\Delta E = qV$$

Since the charge (electron, $q = -e$) is the same for all components, the greatest energy change occurs across the component with the greatest voltage drop.

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 1 — What determines voltage drop?}

In a series circuit: $V \propto R$. The largest resistor has the largest voltage drop.

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 2 — Conclusion.}

The electron has the greatest energy change moving through the largest resistor (greatest voltage drop).

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} Water loses the most gravitational energy dropping through the tallest waterfall (largest height difference = largest voltage).
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

The \textbf{hill diagram} is a powerful tool for visualising potential. Think of a circuit as a hill for electrons:

\bigskip
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.9]
\draw[->] (0,0) -- (10,0) node[right] {along circuit};
\draw[->] (0,0) -- (0,6) node[above] {Potential $V$};
\draw[dashed, blue] (1,5) -- (9,5) node[right, blue] {High potential (positive terminal)};
\draw[dashed, red] (1,1) -- (9,1) node[right, red] {Low potential (negative terminal)};
\draw[very thick, black] (1,5) -- (4,5) -- (4,3) node[midway,left] {Battery};
\draw[very thick, black] (4,3) -- (6,3) node[midway,above] {Resistor};
\draw[very thick, black] (6,3) -- (9,3) -- (9,1);
\draw[very thick, black] (9,1) -- (1,1);
\draw[arrows=->] (4.5,5.3) -- (4.5,3.3) node[midway,right] {$E = \mathcal{E}$};
\draw[arrows=->] (6.3,3.3) -- (6.3,1.3) node[midway,right] {$V = IR$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

\bigskip
\begin{itemize}
    \item Electrons \textbf{gain energy} going \emph{against the electric field} through the battery (from low to high potential).
    \item Electrons \textbf{lose energy} going \emph{with the electric field} through a resistor (from high to low potential).
    \item The height of the hill = potential energy per unit charge (voltage).
\end{itemize}

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Q17 (HKDSE Ch2 MC):} The figure shows a ``hill diagram'' of part of a circuit. What does the height of the diagram represent?

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item Potential energy of electrons
    \item Kinetic energy of electrons
    \item Potential energy of positive charges
    \item Kinetic energy of positive charges
\end{enumerate}

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

The hill diagram shows \textbf{electric potential} — the potential energy per unit positive charge at each point.

For electrons: potential energy $= qV = (-e)V$. The height is proportional to this.

But by convention, we define potential for positive test charges: height = potential energy of positive charges.

\bigskip
\textbf{Answer: (c)} Potential energy of positive charges (i.e. electric potential $V$ = energy per unit positive charge).
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=blue!5,leftline=true,linecolor=blue,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{Color-code equipotential wires:} All wires at the same potential get the same color. In the hill diagram, horizontal lines at the same height are at the same potential. Points connected by a wire (with no component in between) are at the same potential.
\end{mdframed}

\bigskip

% ------------------------------------------------------------
% Section 9: Series vs Parallel — Brightness and Current
% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section{9. Series vs Parallel — The Brightness Question}

When bulbs are arranged differently, why do they shine differently? Let's answer this through problems.

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Q22 (HKDSE Ch2 MC):} A light bulb is connected to a battery. In which case would the light bulb be the dimmest?

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item Connect a low-resistance resistor in series with the bulb.
    \item Connect a high-resistance resistor in series with the bulb.
    \item Connect a low-resistance resistor in parallel with the bulb.
    \item Connect a high-resistance resistor in parallel with the bulb.
\end{enumerate}

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

The bulb is dimmest when it dissipates the least power.

\bigskip
\textbf{Series case:} Adding any resistor in series increases total $R$, so current $I = V/R$ decreases. $P_{\text{bulb}} = I^2 R_{\text{bulb}}$ decreases. A \textbf{high-$R$} series resistor causes more dimming than a low-$R$ one.

\bigskip
\textbf{Parallel case:} The bulb still sees the full battery voltage (in parallel, voltage across each branch is the same). The extra parallel resistor draws some current away, but the bulb's voltage and power are unchanged.

\bigskip
\textbf{Answer: (b)} A high-resistance resistor in series causes the greatest reduction in current, making the bulb dimmest.

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} Put a narrow pipe in series with the waterwheel. The narrower the pipe, the less water gets through, and the dimmer the waterwheel. In parallel, the waterwheel still sees full pump pressure — the extra pipe just diverts some water without changing the wheel's pressure.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

Key comparison:

\bigskip
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{p{4cm} p{4.5cm} p{4.5cm}}
\toprule
 & \textbf{Series} & \textbf{Parallel} \\
\midrule
Current & Same through all & Splits: $I_{\text{total}} = I_1 + I_2$ \\
\midrule
Voltage & Splits: $V_{\text{total}} = V_1 + V_2$ & Same across all branches \\
\midrule
Resistance & $R_{\text{eq}} = R_1 + R_2$ & $1/R_{\text{eq}} = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2$ \\
\midrule
Brightness & $P = I^2R$ (larger $R$ = brighter) & $P = V^2/R$ (smaller $R$ = brighter) \\
\midrule
One fails & All go out & Others keep working \\
\midrule
Water analogy & One pipe with multiple narrow sections & One main pipe splitting into two branches \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Q (HKDSE Ch2 MC):} The light bulbs in the circuit are all identical. Which statements are correct?

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*)]
    \item Bulbs W and X have the same brightness.
    \item Bulbs Y and Z have the same brightness.
    \item Bulb Y is brighter than bulb W.
\end{enumerate}

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

\begin{itemize}
    \item Y and Z are in series $\Rightarrow$ same current $\Rightarrow$ same power $\Rightarrow$ same brightness. \textbf{Statement (2) is true.}
    \item W and X are in parallel $\Rightarrow$ same voltage $\Rightarrow$ same power $\Rightarrow$ same brightness. \textbf{Statement (1) is true.}
    \item The parallel branch (W and X) gets half the current of the series branch (Y and Z combined). Each of W and X gets $I/2$, while Y and Z each get $I$. Since $P \propto I^2$, Y is brighter than W. \textbf{Statement (3) is true.}
\end{itemize}

\bigskip
\textbf{Answer: (d)} All three statements are correct.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

% ------------------------------------------------------------
% Section 10: Short Circuit and Open Circuit
% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section{10. Short Circuit and Open Circuit — What Goes Wrong?}

Let's understand what happens when things go wrong.

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Q36 (HKDSE Ch2 MC):} In the circuit below, what is the reading of the voltmeter when both switches S1 and S2 are open?

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

When both switches are open, no current flows through the circuit (open circuit = infinite resistance).

The voltmeter, connected across the battery, measures the full battery EMF.

\bigskip
\textbf{Answer: 6 V} (or the battery emf, depending on connection).

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} Open all valves — no water flows. The pressure gauge reads the full pump pressure.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Q37 (HKDSE Ch2 MC):} In the circuit shown, what is the reading of the voltmeter when both switches S1 and S2 are closed?

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

When both switches are closed, they act as wires (0 $\Omega$ resistance).

A closed switch in parallel with a component short-circuits that component — the component has $V = 0$ across it.

The voltmeter, connected across the shorted component, reads 0 V.

\bigskip
\textbf{Answer: 0 V.}

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} Close the valve across the waterwheel — water bypasses the wheel through the open pipe. The pressure across the wheel becomes zero.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

Key definitions:

\bigskip
\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=red!5,leftline=true,linecolor=red,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{Short circuit ($R = 0$):} Zero-resistance path bypasses a component. All current takes this path instead. $V = 0$ across the shorted component.

\textbf{DANGER:} A short circuit across a battery: $I = V/R = V/0 \to \infty$. The battery delivers enormous power — overheating, possible fire.

\bigskip
\textbf{Open circuit ($R \to \infty$):} Broken path. Zero current flows. Any component in series with the break has $I = 0$.
\end{mdframed}

\bigskip

% ------------------------------------------------------------
% Section 11: Problem-Solving Strategy
% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section{11. The Water-First Strategy — How to Solve Any Circuit Problem}

Whenever you face a circuit problem, follow these steps:

\bigskip

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=purple!5,leftline=true,linecolor=purple,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{The Water-First Strategy:}

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{Step \arabic*:},itemsep=8pt,topsep=0pt]
    \item \textbf{Read and draw.} Read the problem. Draw the circuit (even if one is given, redraw it). Next to it, draw the water analogy.
    \item \textbf{Color-code equipotential wires.} All wires at the same potential get the same color. This reveals parallel branches immediately.
    \item \textbf{Isolate each component.} For each resistor, draw it separately. Label the voltage across it ($V$) and the current through it ($I$). Then apply $V = IR$.
    \item \textbf{Find the topology.} Are resistors in series (same current) or parallel (same voltage)?
    \item \textbf{Simplify step by step.} Combine the simplest pair first. Work toward a single equivalent resistance.
    \item \textbf{Work backwards.} Find the total current. Then distribute it to each branch (series = same $I$, parallel = $V/R$).
    \item \textbf{Check energy.} Total EMF = sum of all PDs. Total power in = total power out.
    \item \textbf{Ask: water analogy?} At each step, ask: would the water system behave this way?
\end{enumerate}
\end{mdframed}

\bigskip

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Q6 (HKDSE Ch2 MC):} All resistors in the circuit are identical. The ammeter reads 1.0 A. Find the current through the battery.

\bigskip
\textbf{Solution}

Apply the strategy:

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 1 — Identify topology.} With identical resistors, the total current depends on how many parallel branches exist.

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 2 — Simplify.} For $n$ identical resistors in parallel:
$$R_{\text{eq}} = R/n$$

Total current $I_{\text{total}} = n \times I_{\text{branch}}$.

\bigskip
\textbf{Step 3 — Apply to the problem.} If the ammeter reads 1.0 A in one branch, and there are $n$ identical parallel branches:
$$I_{\text{total}} = n \times 1.0\text{ A}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Water analogy:} If one pipe in a split carries 1.0 L/s and there are $n$ identical pipes in parallel, the total flow is $n$ L/s.
\end{exercise}

\bigskip

% ------------------------------------------------------------
% Section 12: Quick Reference Formula Sheet
% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section{12. Quick Reference — All Formulas in One Place}

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=yellow!10,leftline=true,linecolor=yellow!60!black,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{Charge and Current}
$$\boxed{I = \frac{Q}{t} \quad Q = It}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Voltage and EMF}
$$\boxed{V = \frac{W}{Q} \quad \text{EMF} = \frac{\text{energy supplied by battery}}{Q}}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Ohm's Law}
$$\boxed{V = IR \quad I = \frac{V}{R} \quad R = \frac{V}{I}}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Resistivity}
$$\boxed{R = \frac{\rho\ell}{A}}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Equivalent Resistance}
$$\boxed{R_{\text{eq}}(\text{series}) = R_1 + R_2 + \cdots}$$
$$\boxed{\frac{1}{R_{\text{eq}}}(\text{parallel}) = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \cdots}$$
$$\boxed{R_{\text{eq}}(2\text{ parallel}) = \frac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2}}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Power}
$$\boxed{P = VI = I^2R = \frac{V^2}{R}}$$
$$\boxed{E = Pt}$$

\bigskip
\textbf{Water Analogy Cheat Sheet}
\begin{tabular}{p{3cm} p{5.5cm}}
$I$ & Flow rate (L/s) \\
$V$ & Pressure difference \\
$R$ & Narrowness of pipe \\
$P$ & Pressure $\times$ flow rate \\
Battery & Pump \\
Voltmeter & Pressure gauge (parallel) \\
Ammeter & Flow meter (series) \\
Short circuit & Burst pipe \\
Open circuit & Closed valve \\
\end{tabular}
\end{mdframed}

\bigskip

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=green!5,leftline=true,linecolor=green,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{Color-coding rule:} When drawing circuits, use the same color for all wires connected to the positive terminal of the battery. Use a different color for all wires connected to the negative terminal. Use a third color for earthed points. This makes parallel branches visually obvious.
\end{mdframed}

\end{document}

\section{A Reliable Method for Mixed Problems}

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=green!5,leftline=true,linecolor=green!60!black,linewidth=2pt]
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{Step \arabic*:},itemsep=5pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{Redraw the operating circuit.} Replace closed switches and ideal ammeters by wires; remove open branches and ideal voltmeters.
  \item \textbf{Mark nodes.} Every continuous ideal wire is one potential. Components sharing both end nodes are parallel.
  \item \textbf{Reduce resistance from the inside out.} Keep the original circuit visible.
  \item \textbf{Find total current.} Use $I_{\rm total}=\mathcal E/R_{\rm total}$ for an ideal source, or include internal resistance.
  \item \textbf{Work backwards.} Series: same current. Parallel: same voltage. Use $V=IR$ on one component at a time.
  \item \textbf{Check conservation.} Junction currents balance; rises and drops around a loop balance; source power equals total load power for an ideal circuit.
\end{enumerate}
\end{mdframed}

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Final check problem (adapted from Success Key Q30).} A 3.0 V ideal battery is connected to three identical $2\,\Omega$ resistors. One resistor is in series with two resistors in parallel. Find (a) battery current, (b) current in either parallel branch, and (c) p.d. across the parallel pair.

\textbf{Solution.}
\[
R_p=\frac{2}{2}=1\,\Omega,
\qquad R_{\rm total}=2+1=3\,\Omega.
\]
Thus
\[
I_{\rm battery}=\frac{3.0}{3}=\boxed{1.0\text{ A}}.
\]
The two identical branches share current equally, so each carries $\boxed{0.50\text{ A}}$. Their common p.d. is
\[
V_p=(0.50)(2)=\boxed{1.0\text{ V}}.
\]
Check: the series resistor drops $(1.0)(2)=2.0$ V, and $2.0+1.0=3.0$ V.
\end{exercise}

\section{Quick Reference and Exam Checks}

\begin{center}
{\small
\noindent\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{p{34mm} X X}
\toprule
\textbf{Quantity} & \textbf{Definition / formula} & \textbf{Unit and meaning} \\
\midrule
Current & $I=Q/t$ & A; charge flow per second \\
Potential difference & $V=W/Q$ & V; energy transferred per coulomb \\
EMF & $\mathcal E=W_{\rm supplied}/Q$ & V; energy supplied per coulomb \\
Resistance & $R=V/I$ & $\Omega$ \\
Uniform wire & $R=\rho\ell/A$ & $\rho$ in $\Omega\,\mathrm m$ \\
Power & $P=VI=I^2R=V^2/R$ & W; energy transferred per second \\

\end{tabularx}}
\end{center}

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=yellow!10,leftline=true,linecolor=yellow!60!black,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{Ten-second answer check}
\begin{itemize}[itemsep=2pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item Is a parallel equivalent resistance smaller than every branch?
  \item Do branch currents add to the total current?
  \item Do potential drops add to the source emf around a complete loop?
  \item Does an ideal wire have zero p.d. along it?
  \item Is the ammeter in series and the voltmeter in parallel?
  \item Did you use area proportional to diameter squared in $R=\rho\ell/A$?
  \item For power comparisons, did you identify whether current or voltage is common?
\end{itemize}
\end{mdframed}

\begin{mdframed}[backgroundcolor=red!5,leftline=true,linecolor=red,linewidth=2pt]
\textbf{Language that earns physics marks}
\begin{itemize}[itemsep=2pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item Say ``the same current flows through series components,'' not ``current is shared.''
  \item Say ``parallel branches have the same p.d.,'' not ``they have the same current.''
  \item Say ``the source supplies energy to charge'' and ``the resistor converts electrical energy.''
